claims.text: The study concerns Q235 steel in a pre-exposure state without prior surface treatment or coating.
Exposure at elevated temperature and controlled oxygen partial pressure promotes formation of a stable passive oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Formation of the stable passive oxide layer suppresses the onset of corrosion-related degradation.
At 300°C and an oxygen partial pressure of approximately 0.2 atm, the steel surface reacts with oxygen to form an oxide layer.
The oxide formed under the proposed conditions is dense and adherent.
The oxide layer is likely composed of Fe3O4, Fe2O3, or both.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation and corrosion.
Q235 steel exposed at 300°C and 0.2 atm oxygen will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than untreated Q235 steel exposed to ambient air at room temperature.
The proposed mechanism is applicable between oxygen partial pressures of 0.1 and 0.3 atm.
The proposed mechanism is applicable at temperatures up to 400°C.
Aggressive chemical species such as chlorides may prevent the proposed protective behavior.
Temperatures exceeding the oxide layer's thermal stability may prevent the proposed protective behavior.
The exact oxide composition and its protective properties under the proposed conditions are not fully characterized.
An inert-atmosphere treatment at 300°C can serve as a control for distinguishing oxygen-dependent oxide formation from temperature exposure alone.
Failure to observe either a lower corrosion rate or a stable oxide layer under controlled oxygen exposure would falsify the hypothesis.
